findings.title: Lineage endpoints bypass streams role gate (CWE-862)
findings.why_it_matters: Every endpoint in app/api/v1/streams.py gates on require_roles(user, "DESIGNER", "PROCESS_CONTROLLER", "SYSTEM_ADMIN") — GET /streams/{id} included (streams.py:443). The three lineage endpoints gate only on a valid token plus project membership (has_project_access); they never call require_roles. Before this diff the streams record_type branch of /graph and /downstream always ended in 404 (data_lineage never contains record_type='streams' — the diff's own docstring says so), so the lineage path exposed nothing about a stream. This diff adds the streams branch with a synthetic root that serializes the stream's own fields (source, created_by, created_at) plus the downstream calc-lineage rows (record_type/record_id/change_summary/actor_user_id). A project member holding a role outside the streams allow-list (REVIEWER is an LDAP-mapped role in the default ldap_group_role_map; CHECKER and VIEWER are in current_actor's _ALLOWED_ROLES) gets 403 on GET /streams/{id} but 200 with stream metadata and calc-lineage content from GET /lineage/streams/{id}/graph. That is a broken-access-control path around a role gate that the owning module deliberately applies, and it also widens what a low-privilege project member can enumerate about calc results.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/api/v1/lineage.py:137 — `    user: Annotated[_Actor, Depends(current_actor)],` (the /graph endpoint's only authz: current_actor + project guard; no require_roles anywhere in lineage.py — grep for require_roles in that file returns nothing, and its import line is `from app.api.v1.config import _Actor, current_actor`)

pcs-backend/app/api/v1/streams.py:443 — `    require_roles(user, "DESIGNER", "PROCESS_CONTROLLER", "SYSTEM_ADMIN")` (get_stream's role gate; the same call appears on every one of the 18 streams endpoints)

pcs-backend/app/api/v1/lineage.py:320 — `        "source": stream.source,` (new synthetic root serializes stream fields; lineage.py:323 — `        "actor_user_id": str(stream.created_by) if stream.created_by else None,`)

diff-backend-app.txt new branch in graph(): `+    if record_type == "streams":` → `+        return await _stream_graph(session, record_id, max_depth=max_depth)` — pre-diff this path fell through to tracker.latest(record_type='streams') which finds no rows and raises 404, i.e. the diff is what first makes stream data reachable through the lineage module

pcs-backend/app/api/v1/lineage.py:190 — `        "change_summary": lineage.change_summary,` — the downstream rows returned by the new streams branch carry free-text change summaries and calc record ids
findings.suggested_fix: Add the same role gate the streams module applies to the lineage endpoints, e.g. in app/api/v1/lineage.py add `from app.api.v1.config import require_roles` and call `require_roles(user, "DESIGNER", "PROCESS_CONTROLLER", "SYSTEM_ADMIN")` at the top of upstream(), downstream() and graph() (before _guard_record_access, so the guard stays the outermost check per the batch's hard constraint). Assumption: the intended role model for the lineage surface is the streams-module allow-list; if the product instead intends any project member to read lineage, then the streams endpoints' role list is the thing to reconcile — either way the two surfaces should agree, and the choice should be recorded in docs/PCS-UI-SPEC.md §7.7.2. The fail-closed 404 shape for cross-project/unknown-type must stay byte-identical after the change.

findings.title: current_user path skips new account-status check (CWE-613)
findings.why_it_matters: The diff's stated invariant is that account status is judged in exactly one place — the actor layer — so that 'disabling takes effect immediately' holds globally (config.py docstring: '一处判定，全局生效'). But there is a second authentication entry point in the same app: current_user (auth.py:149), which returns the raw JWT payload dict and is used by GET /auth/me (auth.py:287) and six /meta endpoints (meta.py:162,171,179,192,200,213). Those paths never call is_account_disabled, so a user disabled while holding an unexpired access token still gets 200 from /auth/me and from the meta endpoints. No data of another user is exposed (the response is the caller's own username/role/user_id), so the impact is limited — but the frontend's session probe is /auth/me, so a disabled user still sees a 'logged in' session while every data call 401s with USER_DISABLED, and the new invariant is not actually global. It is a gap in the diff's own design claim rather than a pre-existing bug in the endpoints.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/api/v1/auth.py:287 — `    user: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(current_user)],` (GET /auth/me authenticates through current_user, which never touches users.status)
pcs-backend/app/api/v1/meta.py:162 — `    _user: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(current_user)],` (six /meta endpoints share the same status-blind dependency)
pcs-backend/app/api/v1/config.py:563 — `    if await is_account_disabled(db, user_id=user_id):` — the only status check introduced by this diff, reachable solely through current_actor
pcs-backend/app/api/v1/auth.py:149 — `def current_user(authorization: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None) -> dict[str, Any]:` — a second, parallel authentication dependency with no DB access
findings.suggested_fix: Make the status check apply to the second entry point as well: either give current_user an `db: Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_db)]` parameter and call `is_account_disabled(db, user_id=_derive_user_id(payload))` before returning the payload, or (smaller blast radius) have /auth/me and the /meta endpoints depend on current_actor instead of current_user. Assumption: /auth/me must keep working for non-production mock logins, which is satisfied because is_account_disabled returns False when the users row is absent. If the product decides the session-probe path should stay available for disabled users (to let the frontend render the 'account disabled' screen), record that as an explicit exemption in ADR-0046 §⑤ instead of leaving the two paths silently divergent.

residual_risks: Fail-open by construction on missing users rows: is_account_disabled queries `User.user_id == <token user_id claim>` and returns False when no row matches. Two consequences I could not rule out from code alone: (a) legacy account rows whose user_id != uuid5(NAMESPACE_DNS, username) (the shape TODO-137 tracks) are invisible to the check — the derived id has no row — so a disabled legacy account keeps full access until the row is migrated; the repo's release checklist requires `SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE user_id <> uuid5_derived(username)` = 0, which makes this a deployment precondition rather than a code defect; (b) if the users table is empty or the AD sync never ran, the whole 'disabling takes effect immediately' feature degrades silently to pass-everything with no startup assertion or metric to reveal it.

users.status is a free VARCHAR(20) with no CHECK constraint restricting it to ACTIVE/DISABLED (app/models/project.py:157). is_account_disabled only compares against UserStatus.DISABLED.value, so a NULL status or any typo'd value is treated as 'not disabled' (fail-open). No code path writes such a value today (admin_user_service writes the enum value), so this is a data-integrity gap rather than a live bypass.

The mock-login double gate is only as strong as the two conditions it combines: `is_production` is an exact string compare (`self.env == "production"`, app/core/config.py:129) and the shipped pcs-backend/.env.example sets `PCS_ENABLE_MOCK_LOGIN=true`. A deployment that copies the example file and sets ENV to anything other than exactly 'production' (e.g. 'prod', 'Production') both mounts the mock router and passes the new second gate — leaving mock-login live, which issues a SYSTEM_ADMIN token for 'dan'. This exposure is pre-existing (the router-mount decision and is_production are untouched by the diff), and the diff's second gate does not compensate for it because the example file turns that gate on; I did not file it as a finding for that reason, but the 'double gate' should not be read as defence-in-depth while .env.example ships the switch enabled.

The WebSocket handshake accepts the bearer token as a query parameter (?token=), which puts credentials into access logs and proxy logs (CWE-532). ws.py is touched by this diff and the _authenticate function was rewritten, but the token transport itself is unchanged and I found no frontend caller of /api/v1/ws/notifications, so I could not establish live exposure.

callsite completeness: my sweep of current_actor's callers was grep-only over pcs-backend/app (no symbol-aware search was available in this session), so I cannot exclude a dynamically-bound or re-exported call site that would now receive a coroutine instead of an actor, nor a non-app/ caller (scripts/, worker) that calls current_actor directly.

The new per-request users.status lookup adds one DB round trip to every authenticated request (current_actor runs on all 18 streams endpoints plus the config/util/supplier/workspaces surfaces). I did not evaluate the resulting query-load amplification or lock behaviour under concurrency; that is a performance/reliability question I left to the performance and reliability reviewers.
testing_gaps: No test pins the role model across the two surfaces: the new tests cover the disabled-account 401 and the cross-project 404, but nothing asserts what a non-streams-allow-list role (REVIEWER/CHECKER/VIEWER) gets from GET /lineage/streams/{id}/graph versus GET /streams/{id}. A test asserting 'REVIEWER ⇒ 403 on both, or ⇒ 200 on both by an explicit decision' would pin whichever answer is intended and would have caught the current divergence.

No test covers the disabled check against a users row whose user_id is not the derived uuid5(NAMESPACE_DNS, username) (the TODO-137 legacy shape), nor against a NULL/unrecognised status value — both currently evaluate to 'not disabled'. A test that documents the intended outcome (reject vs pass) for those rows would either close the hole or make the fail-open explicit.

No test exercises GET /auth/me (or the /meta endpoints) with a DISABLED account's existing access token, so the divergence between current_user and current_actor on account status is untested and would not be caught by a future refactor of either dependency.

The mock-login gate tests cover the PCS_ENABLE_MOCK_LOGIN env-var name and the production RuntimeError, but there is no test that a non-production deployment with the switch ON still refuses when is_production is true via the router-level path, nor that the startup assertion actually trips when the mock router is mounted in a production-configured app (the OpenAPI-path check depends on FastAPI's lazy-mount behaviour, which no test in the diff exercises).
